questions.question: Explain why South Africa must manage its energy, defining the greener economy and the role of energy efficiency in reaching it.
questions.expected_answer: Three pressures make management unavoidable. Supply: the load-shedding years proved demand can outrun a strained system, and the fastest relief is lower, smarter demand — a new station takes a decade, efficiency takes a season. Climate and trade: South Africa is among the most carbon-intensive economies per unit of output because roughly 80 per cent of electricity is coal-made, so Paris Agreement commitments and arriving carbon border taxes — under which exports made with dirty electricity pay penalties at rich-country borders — turn the grid's carbon into a cost on every exported product. Equity: millions of households spend painful shares of income on energy and clinics and schools fail without reliable power, so wasted energy is development lost. A greener economy is one that keeps growing while its resource use and emissions shrink — decoupling prosperity from pollution — and sustainable lifestyles are the household mirror of the same idea. Energy efficiency is the master lever: getting the same service from less energy. It is called the invisible power station because saving a station's worth of demand is cheaper, faster and cleaner than building one — the kilowatt-hour never used is the cheapest and cleanest one there is.

questions.question: Describe the responsibilities of government and of businesses in managing South Africa's energy toward a greener economy, with named instruments and practices.
questions.expected_answer: Government holds the levers of law, tax, planning and example. It sets the Integrated Resource Plan — the official roadmap of what retires and what gets built by which year — runs the REIPPPP auctions that procure renewable plants, and restructures Eskom so an independent grid company can carry many competing producers. It prices carbon through Africa's first carbon tax, designs tariffs that reward off-peak use, and writes the quiet rules that save more than headline projects: building energy-performance regulations, appliance labelling and minimum efficiency standards. It delivers directly — subsidised solar water heaters and efficient lighting for poor households, free basic electricity — channels Just Energy Transition Partnership finance into grid building, coal-town retraining and green industry, and leads by example through public-building retrofits and clean procurement. Business consumes most of the country's energy, so its choices weigh heaviest: energy audits trace where joules are wasted — compressed-air leaks, worn motors, uninsulated pipes — and rank profitable fixes; firms self-generate with rooftop and utility-scale solar and wind, using wheeling to move power across the grid between their sites; and supply-chain pressure — carbon footprint reporting, European border carbon rules, investor climate screening — has made clean energy a condition of market access. The counterweight duty is avoiding greenwashing: real management is measured — baseline, target, audit, report.

questions.question: Discuss the responsibilities of individuals in achieving sustainable lifestyles, ranking household actions by impact, and evaluate honestly what individual action can and cannot achieve.
questions.expected_answer: Actions rank by the size of the energy they touch. Water heating first: the electric geyser is the hungriest machine in a typical home, often around 40 per cent of the bill — thermostat to 60 degrees, an insulating geyser blanket, a timer, and ultimately a solar water heater or heat pump so the sun does the heaviest job. Then seasonal heating and cooking: seal and insulate before heating, warm the person rather than the room, cook with lids, pressure cookers and microwaves, and run full loads. Lighting is the cheap certain victory — LEDs give the same light for about a tenth of the electricity. Kill standby power, and count transport: lift clubs, public transport and walking are energy management with a fuel gauge. Beyond the meter sits the citizen layer: shifting use off the evening peak helps the whole grid, rooftop PV and solar geysers turn homes into micro power stations, and civic support for the plants, lines and transition plans decides whether infrastructure gets built. The honest evaluation: individual action alone cannot decarbonise a coal grid — no household can build a transmission line or tax carbon — but the evening peak, the grid's breaking point, is literally the sum of household choices landing together, and the load-shedding years proved that sum can move. Sustainable lifestyle is the name for making the movable sum smaller, inside the rules government writes and the systems business builds.
